utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. At the outset of today's hearing, the Chamber wishes to issue an oral decision concerning one witness who is scheduled to give evidence this week. The Chamber is seised of the Prosecution's 92 bis and 92 ter motion for the five witnesses filed confidentially on the 26th of April this year in which the Prosecution inter alia seeks that evidence of witness 65 ter number 139, a proposed 92 bis witness, be instead admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter and hereby renders its decision insofar as Witness 139 is concerned. The Prosecution submits that the evidence of Witness 139 -- sorry, relates to the situation in Bratunac following the fall of Srebrenica, and that, in light of the specific factual challenges raised by the accused in his pre-trial brief and the positions he has otherwise taken in respect of core facts alleged in the indictment, his evidence would most efficiently and effectively be presented pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The Prosecution further submits that the accused would be able to put his case to, and fully cross-examine this witness. In his response, filed on the 26th of May, 2010, the accused did not oppose this particular request. The Chamber considers that it would be in the interest of justice to receive the proposed evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter, subject to the tendering of transcripts reflecting the official record. The Chamber therefore grants the request and provisionally admits Witness 139's evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter. In addition, the Chamber notes that there are no protective measures currently in place for this witness and that the Chamber is not seised of any motion in this respect. Now we should turn to the continuation of the evidence of the last witness. He should be brought in. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Just a quick update for the Trial Chamber regarding the continual translations. The B/C/S translation of 65 ter 6287, which is P242, has been uploaded into e-court. That had been previously MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. The document will be received as an Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, please sit down. I would like to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. And Mr. Tolimir has some more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May there be peace in this house for all those present, and this trial. And may God's will be done in these proceedings. And may the outcome be as God wishes and not as wish. I would like to bid Mr. Franken good afternoon, and I hope that he will be comfortable here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would now like us to continue where we stopped last time. Let me remind you where it was. You were trying to explain the position vis-à-vis the Defence of the enclave, and you said that you did not side with any of the factions but that you simply defended the enclave. At page 62, when I asked you about Colonel Brantz with whom you were on good terms, as you stated yourself, you said Charlie Brantz is a Dutch Colonel from the north-east sector command. In fact, he was our higher echelon in the staff of the unit, that was, in fact, our higher echelon, and because we knew each other from before, from the Netherlands, it was easier for us to be on good terms with him, quite unlike the situation that would be if he had been somebody else from the international community we did not know. Now, my question is, first of all, I would like us to look at D2. It's a document dated the 12th of July, 1995. It's a document generated by the BH Army, signed by Brigadier Enver Hadzihasanovic. And it details his conversations with Colonel Brantz in the corps command. And let me read from this document, and then I would like you to give me some answers in the context of what we discussed last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please tell us which part of this document you will read? It makes it easier for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, yeah, we can see here -- we need paragraph 4, although I can't see it here in its entirety. I will quote from it, because it flows on to the next page. Could you just move it a little bit to the right so that I can read it. Just a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ah, to the right. On the left side, we can't see the whole document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "At 800 hours this morning, the commander of UNPROFOR for the north-east, Colonel Brantz, paid us a visit. The subject was the current situation in Srebrenica. Brantz briefed us that the forces of the Dutch Battalion and the BH Army managed, in a joint effort, to defend Srebrenica on Monday, and that NATO air support was approved at 0445 hours yesterday." As you can see, this was written on the 12th of July by General Enver Hadzihasanovic, the Chief of the General Staff, and he had talks with Colonel Brantz. Now, I want to ask you this: Whether this report by Enver Hadzihasanovic sent to the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 1st Corps command is in line with what you stated at page 80, lines 14 and 15, where you state clearly, and I quote: "Again, I disagree with you regarding your conclusion that UNPROFOR took sides when it comes to my battalion. I am explaining this again, and I don't think that what we did was tantamount to siding with one of the factions." So I've now read all this out to you. This was a rather comprehensive introduction to my question. I would like to ask you to comment on all this, and I would like to ask you whether this was, indeed, your position and whether you agreed with the colonel when it came to the defence of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my former statement is, that I am not -- I still disagree on the conclusion that UNPROFOR, being, in this case, DutchBat III, took side in my question. I remember saying, and when I'm right, that I do not know how my higher echelons put that in the words or in words. Then again, if you see the report of the BiH general, he speaks of a joint effort to defend Srebrenica. As far as I can see, he refers to the attack of the VRS on the city itself, which we -- on which we responded by starting firing upon the VRS. In that time, BiH was still present, and, of course, they were firing as well on the VRS. And that is not in contradiction what I said before when I tried to explain to you that, in my view, there was no co-ordination or co-operation. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like you to give me a direct answer to my question. Well, I asked several questions and you answered to the best of your abilities. But it says here: "Brantz briefed us that that the forces of the Dutch Battalion and the BH Army succeeded, in a joint, effort to defend Srebrenica on Monday." What you've just told us, how can it be reconciled with what Colonel Brantz told the Chief of the Main Staff of the BH Army on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, again, I'll try to use other words. He refers to a joint effort, and I think that he referred to that attack I described to you in my former answer. You could use that word; and, again, I do not know whether he used these words, because this is a message of the BiH general who probably uses his own words. So I don't know whether Colonel Brantz really said that. But, again, you can't speak of a joint effort when there are three parties in a location; being VHS attacking Srebrenica, then still parts of the 28th BiH division, and my battalion. The VRS attacks, we opened fire, and the 28th Division opened fire on that same VRS. That doesn't prove that in that action there has been any co-operation or coordination. As I stated before, we had a mutual enemy, being the VRS, and if he is attacking the city of Srebrenica, it's quite clear that both parties - and I mean VRS and DutchBat - opened fire. If you want to conclude then that there must have been any co-ordination or co-operation in that case, again I say there was not any co-ordination, co-operation. Coordination other than that meeting I had in March, as we referred to earlier in my testimony. And co-operation, well, you brought several documents where you could see that there was absolutely no co-operation with the BiH, the opposite. I referred to events at Mike, the killing of my soldier, et cetera. Is this a direct and complete answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I understand your point. But, now, in your answer you said, and I quote: We had a joint enemy, the VRS. We, the Dutch Battalion. Is that so? So how did you have a joint enemy, and why did you consider the Republika Srpska army to be your enemy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm reluctant to intervene so early in the session, but we really have gone over this again and again and again. If General Tolimir wants to spend his limited cross-examination time on this topic, fine, but we are really wasting time. I don't think there's another way that Colonel Franken can answer the same question. He's trying; he said himself, I'll try to use other words. But, frankly, this has been asked and answered and asked and answered, and the answer has been consistent for days now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You heard the objection and the comment of Mr. Thayer, and if I compare your last question with the first question of today, I don't see the difference. You were referring exactly to the answer you have got by the witness already, and you should think about the time you are using in court. Perhaps you move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness has just said, and Mr. Thayer himself heard it, We had a joint enemy and that was the Republika Srpska army, end of quote. Now I want to ask the witness why the Army of Republika Srpska was a joint enemy to him and to the Muslims, and does it not indicate that he and the Muslims were on one side and the Republika Srpska army on the other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you are now repeating the same question again. Let's hear the answer of the witness to this question, but then please not again the same question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With "we" in that sentence, I meant, indeed, the Muslim army and my battalion. That the Army of the Republika Srpska was my enemy was quite clear, and more or less in or around to the order I got from the UN to defend a city against an approaching armed force, being the VRS. And, in general, you defend against an enemy and not against friends. Is that -- just hold; I'm reading. And if you say it does indicate that we are on one side, yes. If you keep on explaining the situation that being there are two parties, one attacking, two of them defending, then we were, the ABiH and UNPROFOR, being my battalion, were on the defending side. So in that sense it could indicate we were on one side. But if it implicates that we had co-ordinated and co-operation of each other, that is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on and move to another field.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, this position that you just explained to us, the Republika Srpska army was my enemy, did it affect your partiality or your possible bias if your evidence here before this Tribunal? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that in my evidence I have any partiality. I explained last week, before, that it is for me not of any interest to which my order to defend the city was referring, whether that would have been the VRS, the ABiH, or some other army. I had order as a soldier to defend it to an approaching party. And I'm giving my answers as factual as possible. So I'm just referring to facts. And if I give an opinion, it is on your request. I'm just giving the facts, so there is, as far as I'm concerned, and I'm watching that, you can't speak of any partiality or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I've asked you, you've given me your answer, and now I'm asking you: On the basis of your evidence, who ordered you to defend the town? Who relayed this order to you personally? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, of course, my CO, the commanding officer of DutchBat. But being briefed by him, I understood it that the order came from, if you want a person, General Nicolai being at the HQ at Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Franken. Now, I would like you to tell us whether Colonel Karremans, your immediate superior, or anyone else from the Dutch Battalion from your command had made any promises to the Muslims that there would be air-strikes against VRS positions and that the UNPROFOR would take part in the effort to defend the town against the Serbs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your first question I thought I answered that last week. In the night from the 10th to the 11th, Colonel Karremans had a meeting with the staff of the 28th Division in the city of Srebrenica, and then he informed them about the air attack and other details which were important for them because they had to be sure that they wouldn't be in a certain area. Perhaps you remember my killing-zone story. Then, secondly, UNPROFOR would take part in the effort to defend the town. I do not know exactly what Colonel Karremans said to the 28th Division, so I can't confirm that. Probably he would have said -- but again that's an assumption - he would have said that DutchBat is going to defend the town, but I don't know what words he used because I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like to ask you to show 1D218. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's a statement by brigadier General Nicolai, Cornelis Nicolai, you mentioned him just now. He gave it on the 18th of November, 1996. Well, we can see the front page of that statement in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, can we look at page 11. We can see that it is probably an authentic signature that's affixed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you able to verify that this is General Nikolai's signature?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a page in English, and I do not know whether that -- you mean the sign on the right bottom side of the document? I can't confirm that is his signature because I really don't know. I never worked during long times directly --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... under the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we will hear this witness, and we will ask him, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, whether he did in fact sign the statement. But let us now look at paragraph 2 of his statement where he says: "I further contacted General Tolimir at 1750 hours. I expressed my deep concern for the situation which was developing in the Srebrenica enclave. I told him that his forces, having penetrated into the enclave, was deemed to be an attack on the safe area and asked him to withdraw his troops to 4 kilometres' distance to the south, which was the original confrontation line. His response was that I expected -- was what I expected, to deny that his troops were attacking into the enclave. I further requested that he order his troops not to use their anti-aircraft guns to attack our helicopter which was already underway to carry out the evacuation of the DutchBat soldier's body." And so on. End of quote. Now, I would like you to tell us, do you know what time-period we are talking about regarding this conversation between General Nicolai and General Tolimir? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I only see a timing, and then I have to guess on which date that would occur. I presume that this could have been on the 10th, as I see the description of the situation that General Nicolai gives, and -- please hold. Yeah, well, that will answer your question, but, again, this is an assumption. It is a timing of 1750 hours. Probably on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it might be helpful just to go to the prior page in the English version of the statement and let Colonel Franken look at that. If you look at the bottom of the prior page, I think we may see a date. That's all General Tolimir needs to do to help the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, could you -- can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see it, sir. I'm just reading it. Yeah, well, I can see it, it's on the 9th now. But it has been 15 years, and my memory is pretty good but. It could cope to a situation on the 10th as well. But I see now it was on the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, I saw that this was on the 9th. But do you remember that you said that on the 9th, the 10th, and the 11th you were fighting the VRS and that it was then that you issued a green order? Yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The green order was issued on the 9th. And as of the 9th or before that, starting with the attack on Echo, we had contact with the VRS. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you in engagement? Did you engage the VRS? Was there fire exchanged between you and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean as of the attack on Echo, yes. Occasionally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now please have a look at paragraph 3, where once again General Nicolai talks about what he said, and he says: "Tolimir decided once again to concentrate his responses on our requests, and he said that VRS was not attacking UNPROFOR or the civilian population in Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you on the same page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I have the correct page in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't think so. We have to move to the next page. Page 11.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 11 in English, and I'm in line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is paragraph 3, the third line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me repeat: "Tolimir again chose to focus his answers to our demands by saying that the VRS was not attacking UNPROFOR nor the civil population in Srebrenica. He did make false allegations that the ABiH were using former UN APCs in the enclave and also using heavy weapons from the enclave. This was not true, as we knew that Colonel Karremans had offered the ABiH their own weapons from the weapon collection point, due to the threatening situation. But the ABiH had declined to take up his offer. Tolimir did say ..." and so on. My question is the following: If, on the 10th, and the Muslims as well, in the area in front of your APCs, attacked the Army of Republika Srpska, was Tolimir lying when he said that both the UNPROFOR and the BH Army were firing against his army from Srebrenica? Because you said that on the 9th, the 10th, and the 11th you were in conflict with the Army of Republika Srpska and that this happened even sometime before that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If your question is that whether there was firing contact with the VRS on the 10th of July, I only can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, please don't touch the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It gives additional noise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Sorry, I didn't see you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, the question, which I presume is based on this statement that General Tolimir is showing to Colonel Franken, does not accurately reflect the statement that he is showing him. And I'll quote from what this statement says: "Tolimir again chose to focus his answers to our demands by saying that the VRS was not attacking UNPROFOR nor the civil population in Srebrenica." The question that General Tolimir just asked was: "Was Tolimir lying when he said that both the UNPROFOR and the BH Army were firing against his army from Srebrenica?" That's different. And if he is going to be citing from the document to ask questions, then he should make it clear when he is citing from the document and then when he is putting a different proposition. Otherwise, he is misleading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, this witness is a very experienced person, not only in military terms but also in testifying before this Court. I think he is capable to answer the question in the way which is helpful for the understanding of the whole case and for the Chamber. Nevertheless, Mr. Tolimir, please be very careful by quoting and phrasing your questions to the witness. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness has answered my question. As he said, on the 10th he was in conflict with the Army of Republika Srpska. This is the time which is covered by the conversation with General Nicolai.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As the witness now mentioned heavy weapons offered by Colonel Karremans to the ABiH, can you tell us whether he handed over these weapons, when did he hand them over, and when did they take them over? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that my CO offered the ABiH the weapons still preserved in a so-called "weapon collection point" that were light and heavy weapons that were in the context of the demilitarisation of the enclave were gathered by DutchBat I and kept there more or less in custody. And I know as well that the ABiH was not interested. So there was not an actual handing over or taking over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have a look at the 12th paragraph on page 3 both in English and in B/C/S. I did not say it correctly, it is page 12, paragraph 3, rather than the other way around. Please excuse me. My legal assistant has just brought this to my attention. Thank you. There it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This paragraph, if you had a look, says: "Then the confusion started. Colonel Karremans was concerned that using close air support, not [as interpreted] only on the attacking front, was not sufficient due to the VRS having the ability to retaliate with their heavy weapons which were situated all around the enclave." Can you see what I'm reading from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. "He wanted an attack to take place on all of the positions of the VRS. During the night, the air operation centre asked Colonel Karremans for all VRS positions. Karremans expected that air-strikes would be carried out the next morning and not the close air support. He contacted the local Bosnian authorities to warn them to be prepared for proper air-strikes. Colonel Karremans did not realise that there was never any consideration given to air-strikes but only to close air support. That night the VRS attack stopped." Can you please describe to us in more detail these contacts which Colonel Karremans had with the Muslim army, considering that we have seen here that when he met General Mladic and told him he had handed over 300 rifles to Muslims. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already -- I think I already answered that question, and, again, it was on the night of the 10th to the 11th where Colonel Karremans, as I said before, visited the staff of the 28th ABiH Division in Srebrenica. There he informed them about the air support. And concerning your last remark, do you mean by that that he, being Colonel Karremans, handed over 300 rifles to the Muslims? If that happened, and I would be very surprised, I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a look at that if we have enough time so you will see that this did happen and that the rifles were handed over to the Muslims, because they were not found and you did not take them with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now show Exhibit P607. It is a statement -- your statement, Mr. Franken, and we'll have a look at page 9 in B/C/S, paragraph 3. And in English version, it's page 7, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see the paragraph now, paragraph 6 on page 7 in the English version. You have probably read it already, so I don't have to read it. It is brief. And so I can ask you questions, I will just say for the purpose of the transcript: "On the evening of the 10th of July, there was a meeting between Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans and the civilian and military authorities in the enclave. The same evening, at the market in Srebrenica, he saw about 1500 BH men in uniform, armed with small weapons. I then gave orders to prepare for the defence of Srebrenica. There was then a discussion about the role of BH in this situation and about filling the gaps in our ranks with them." Can you tell us now, based on what we have just read, where did Colonel Karremans hold the meeting with the Muslims in Srebrenica with their civilian and military authorities, and who of the civilian and military representatives attended the meeting, if you know, and who proposed that the Muslims should fill in the gaps in your ranks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the centre of the city, a post office, a well-known post office. There he saw those 1500 BiH soldiers. In this statement it looks as that was the reason why I gave orders to prepare for the defence, but that was originated on the order I got by the UN to defend Srebrenica; in time there is a parallel. I'm surprised by the word the "gaps in our ranks" because there was never, as far as I know, any discussion about filling gaps in our ranks. Again, this should refer to the March agreement, so to say, where we agreed upon filling the spaces not covered by us between or on the flanks of our positions. As far as I know, there has never been a discussion, at least not by me, about filling gaps in the ranks because that would mean that we had a defensive positions within that position Dutch and BiH soldiers, which was not applicable, was not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether you had a chance to review this statement previously; and, if so, when? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I had a chance to read this statement. I read a lot of them. But if I did, I didn't -- probably I did not see or read over the fact that they use -- "gaps in our ranks" is used. To my view and to my knowledge, that is, as I said, incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wish to be correct concerning both your opinion and the facts. You did give this statement, and the statement was submitted to me by the Prosecution. And I had to prepare for my cross-examination on the basis of it. And it is present here as a fact. I'm just asking you to tell us, Who did you discuss this possibility with, namely that the BH soldiers might fill in the gaps of the UNPROFOR ranks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is, as I stated before, somewhere in March/April, and I discussed that with the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, a man known to me as Ramiz. And I do not recollect his last name; could be Becirevic or something. But with that man, Chief of Staff, 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you agreed then that members of the BH Army might fill in the UNPROFOR ranks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated before, to me never -- to me there has never been spoken about filling up the ranks. There has been -- we spoke about filling up the gaps between our positions, as I stated before. And so there's not -- I can't speak of agreement because it was not proposed by the ABiH as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I wanted to hear the answer of the witness. And as I indicated earlier, this witness is capable even to answer repeated questions. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I recognise that, and I certainly agree with that, Mr. President. Nevertheless, we have General Tolimir repeatedly incorporating into his questions misstatements of fact. This witness testified clearly that there was no discussion about filling in ranks. He builds that into the very next question, I let it go because I can't stand up every time that happens. He gets an answer, and then he repeats that misstatement a second time. And he's going to keep doing it and waste more time, through this method of misstating the record. I understand that Colonel Franken is experienced and is capable of answering the questions, but when we have these types of misleading questions in the record, what happens then is the answer that is given is -- does not make clear whether he is accepting that misstatement of fact. And it should not be a burden upon the witness for every misleading question for the witness to have to correct the General's misleading statement of fact. And we see as an example, I let it go, Colonel Franken answers the question, and then he asks the misleading question again, and then Colonel Franken corrects him the second time around. But now we have a question that could conceivably be read to accept that misleading statement that was not objected to. And I -- again, I'm reluctant to have to do this, but I feel that for the clarity of the record and to not place that burden on the witness I have to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The view of the Chamber, Mr. Thayer, there were some repetitions in your statement as well at the moment. And on the other hand, I would like to repeat the position of the Chamber. You may raise these concerns during your re-examination. On the other hand, it's up to the accused to fill his time in that way or that way. He was -- he has indicated to finish in ten hours, and he has to do that, of course. Not to waste time of the Court. But, on the other hand, if, I think this witness is not in a position to be misleaded by a question. And not the accused is giving evidence, but the witness. And if there's a misstatement in the question, the Chamber is able to realise that. We should continue. And I think both parties should be aware of the fact that he is a witness, an important witness, and we should use his evidence for the best of the Chamber and the whole proceeding. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, I apologise that we have frequent interpretations just like now. I had no bad intentions. You mentioned Becirevic yourself; I then decided to ask you something about that because you mentioned that it could have happened at a certain point. I will now move on to another topic so that we will not waste any more time on this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please show, once again, 1D207. Paragraph 11. It is a document entitled "Interview with Franken" dated the 31st of March, 1999. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before we start reading, let me just ask you: Did you personally, supposing that there would be some air-strikes, receive an information to that effect from someone? And if yes, who did you receive it from? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your first question, would there be some air-strikes, and I think you refer to the 11th of July when those air-strikes were promised, no, and that refers to -- or no, and that is based on the fact that after the attack on OP Echo where all conditions were filled to give us close air support or any air support, it was refused by the UN. Then I did not believe any more that we would get any air support any time. Then the fact that the air-strike on the 11th -- or at least air support on the 11th would take place was given to me by my CO, Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I already got the answer that I wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please show 1D218. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see here that this is a statement given by General Nicolai.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at page 12 of this statement on which Mr. Nicolai says the following. I will quote it once we can see it on the screen. It has to do with what you just mentioned, namely the air-strikes. Here it is. It is paragraph 2 in B/C/S. I think it is paragraph 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says: "The next day, the 11th of July, started with a confusing situation. While Colonel Karremans was waiting for the air-strikes, we were waiting for him, the ground commander, to call in close air support." Close air support; I think this is what the abbreviation stands for. "After some time, the VRS continued their attack. Then there was some misunderstanding between Tuzla, HQ Sector North-East, and DutchBat. I only learned about this later. Karremans made a call for air support but used his normal channel through the Sector HQ at Tuzla and did not call us direct. I was never able to establish why he did this during this very urgent situation." Last time, at the end of your testimony, you explained the situation with the Pakistanis. Now you told us what you thought about the air support. My question is the following: The request for close air support or air-strikes, were you the one who made this request, or was it Colonel Karremans? You said that you did it and that you contacted the HQ in Tuzla, in the opinion of two Pakistanis. Now, here, we can see a different information provided by General Nicolai. Can you please tell us, What is this all about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I take your question literally, it is about air support. But there are a couple of situations, even here, confused. The situation with the Pakistanis was before-done air-support requests in support of the attack on one of the OPs so can't be connected to the air-strikes story on the 11th. That has been on the 9th or something like that. Then I was informed, as I told before, by Colonel Karremans, that he was -- got information from UN that there would be air-strikes next morning. An air-strike needs information where to fly to and what to attack. That is the information I gathered, and that is the request I send to Tuzla because that would have been the normal way, next higher echelon. Now, I might not comment that. Is that an answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. There is only one thing that remains unclear to me, and it's a small matter. You may call it close air support or air-strikes, but was it requested directly from Tuzla, and did you overstep the command of the Sarajevo Sector and therefore General Nicolai as well? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tuzla, just for your information, is a lower echelon than Sarajevo. So overstepping the higher echelon and contact Tuzla is not applicable. The normal echelon that I should contact with all my information would have been Tuzla Sector North-East. During these events, Sarajevo, General Nikolai's staff or General Nicolai in person, made contact to DutchBat, being the CO, Colonel Karremans, and kept on doing that. And the request was not from Tuzla, the request was sent to Tuzla, as I tried to make clear before. The request for the targets that would be attacked in the air-strike on the 11th. And, again, I say air-strike because our position was: We were informed there was an air-strike, so the whole discussion about what kind of planes and who is waiting for who or who thinks that the other one thinks something - and I don't want to add to the confusion - but it looks like that everybody thought that the other party thought something but nobody asked, is in that sense, for us, for me at battalion level at that moment, not interesting. I was informed air-strike is coming in; I presented a list of targets and sent that list of targets to Tuzla, my next higher echelon, Sector North-East.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. Now I would like us -- well, I asked you this because General Nicolai asked this question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 10. Paragraph 4 of the statement made by General Nicolai. That's 1D218. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I hope you can see this paragraph 4 where it says "On Sunday ..." begins with the words "on Sunday." Now we will skip all that. We move on to line 5 in paragraph 4 where it says: "Zagreb made it clear that General Janvier did not want to use this ultimate solution without DutchBat having first used their weapons. He wanted a step to be taken before the calling in of air-strikes. According to the results of those consultations, we gave orders to DutchBat to take blocking positions south of Srebrenica town so that if the VRS attacked the town, this would not only be an attack on the civilian population but also an attack on the UNPROFOR troops. In this case, all the conditions for using air power would be met. This order was carried out by the DutchBat. At the same time we sent a message to the VRS leadership." This is what General Nicolai stated. Is there any mention here of the use of weapons or only of taking blocking positions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the text used there are the words of General Nicolai, and if you want an explanation, then please ask him. The only thing I know that I got order to defend with all means the city of Srebrenica, which is including, with all means, including the use of weapons. The only thing that surprises me that there had been attacks on several OPs, as we mentioned before, and probably -- or I can only conclude that they did not see that as an attack on UNPROFOR, and further on asked General Nicolai.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At any rate, I will do so. But I would just like to ask you to tell me whether you received this order from Nicolai, this order to defend Srebrenica at all costs, or whether somebody else issued this order to you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I heard of it, I was informed by my CO. As I stated before, Colonel Karremans told me that we got ordered to defend the city of Srebrenica. And then I started working on that green order. And later on there was something, or a telegram or something, but whether that was signed or originated by General Nicolai or somebody of his staff or even higher command, I do not recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You will remember that your commander ordered you to open fire on the VRS on the 9th, the 10th, and the 11th; yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander didn't order me. The position was clear, OPs, observation posts, knew that they had to defend, when attacked, had to defend their OPs. And then they open fire. There was one occasion where I repeated that order to use weapons, that is, when the VRS attacked the city of Srebrenica itself. It was reported to me that the VRS infantry was descending from the high grounds in the south, and I ordered commander B Company to open fire. But, in fact, he already knew that he should do that, but that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I kindly ask you for your patience. I need the answer that I want to get. General Nicolai says here: "According to the result of those consultations, we gave orders to DutchBat to take blocking positions south of Srebrenica town so that if the VRS attacked the town, this would not only be an attack on the civilian population but also an attack on UNPROFOR troops."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think there's no need to read this portion again and again. We have it on the screen and on the record and the witness has heard it. We have it on the record and the original document. Please put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, my question on the basis of what I've just read would be this: Was this all about creating conditions on the ground for air-strikes to be carried out, or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the faintest idea. The only thing I know, I was to defend a city. And what the second thoughts or deeper thoughts of my higher, higher echelon was, I was not informed about. I took it that the order to defend the city was to simply prevent the VRS of entering the city. As simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, before the 9th, before issuing the green order, were you in any way involved in the discussion as to how your battalion should act in order to ensure air support or air-strikes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not -- as far as I knew, it was not depending on the acting of my battalion; it was more depending on the actions taken by a aggressor in this case, particularly the VRS. And as I said before, air support could be called in the very moment a UN unit was attacked, and the boundaries of the enclave were passed by the VRS. And there were two other conditions, but I can't recollect them, but they were not important. The fact was, UN attacked, VRS coming into the enclave was given enough reason to ask for air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we have seen what General Janvier thought of that. But now I would like to ask you, on the basis of your answers: Why do you call --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You just mentioned General Janvier; was that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. He said -- well, in fact, I quoted what General Janvier said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were you referring to General Nicolai perhaps, and not to General Janvier?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I meant General Janvier, the UNPROFOR force commander, who said that air-strikes should not be used. And I said Zagreb made it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to avoid any misunderstanding. You were referring to General Janvier. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the transcript, you said the aggressor, VRS, did I understand you correctly? And what do you mean when you say the aggressor, the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I mean is that in case of a status quo, there is a party attacking, then I call him an aggressor. And in this case, it was the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you adopt that term from the Muslims, or would you use the same term for any attack? Would you call any attack an aggression?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is too generalising for me. I can't answer that question. I did not adopt the term from the Muslim. It is a general definition of aggressor. Aggressor is somebody who attacks another party, in my view. And in this case it was the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, of course, you are entitled to your opinion and you can explain your positions and I have nothing against that. But could you please tell me this: When you received the order to take blocking positions to the south, as you've just told us, were you notified in any way of the purpose of taking those blocking positions, and was it one of the preconditions for UNPROFOR to come under an attack to provoke the VRS into attacking them and then to use it as a pretext for calling in air support? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, all kinds of considerations that took place on my higher, higher, and higher echelons I do not know of. Just picking up the order I got, it was the aim of my defensive positions, blocking positions, was to prevent the VRS to enter the city of Srebrenica. And that's it. For me there were no secondary or even further-away reasons to do it. Simple. Defend it. Enemy not coming in to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Your APCs that took the blocking positions, were they dug in, sheltered, or were they out there in the clear as perfect targets for the tanks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to find positions to dig them in. That did not succeed because the kind of ground in that area. We took as much cover as possible, but that was not very successful everywhere because you had to -- have to use your own weapons systems as well, so you couldn't hide them away, as far as is possible with a hail-white vehicle, so they were out in the clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If they were out in the clear, and I have no reason to doubt you there, were they a useful target, and could they have been destroyed with anti-armour weapons or tanks?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they were a useful target, I can't judge that. But they could have been destroyed with anti-armour weapons and tanks with a proper gunner, yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were any vehicles destroyed at those blocking positions that you took there to the south? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, in those blocking positions, two vehicles were damaged by near misses, as far as we could trace back, by a Tango 55. Tango 55, sorry, is a main battle tank used by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you told by your superior command that the VRS ordered its troops not to open fire on UNPROFOR and UNPROFOR combat vehicles? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As you asked me last week, no, I was not aware of the fact that VRS ordered things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have 1D207 up on the screen. It's an interview with Franken. I'm interested in page 1, paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, and what about the previous document, 1D218? Are you tendering it, or do you prefer to tender it with the witness Nikolai?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for reminding me. I would like to tender it into evidence because it will be used in the testimony of General Nikolai before this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D218 will be Exhibit D70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Franken, please look at paragraph 11 on page 1. You say: "Voorhoeve told Karremans that he had to defend the enclave to the extreme but that absolutely no body-bags were allowed to go home. Karremans then asked Voorhoeve, 'Can you tell me, how I am supposed to carry out this defence?' He did not get any answer from this question to the minister, however." So could you please tell us who is Voorhoeve and what his function was and whether he was your superior in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Voorhoeve was the minister of defence of the Netherlands. And in my chain of command, but I suggest you mean the chain of command for DutchBat, my chain of command was very easy; there was my CO, of course, and there it ended. But the chain of command for DutchBat, he had no position because we were in the command of the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, please don't touch the microphone again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm doing it again. I'm very sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, now, could you tell us whether the Dutch defence minister overstepped his authority when he issued orders to you, given that you were part of the UN chain of command, and whether you were actually duty-bound to comply with his orders? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be clear, what was meant here that within the context of the order to defend the city of Srebrenica, the minister had obviously some restraints. He did not order us to defend it in that way, but he knew, of course, about that. Just reading. Well, you can't step -- overstep an authority which you do not have, because he didn't have any authority within the UN chain of command. If you had formally -- if he wished something, he, theoretically, had to bring that in in the top of the UN line, and not directly to the commander of DutchBat, of course. And I was not duty-bound to comply his orders. But then again, I was not in discussion with him. I was not the receiver of these guide-lines. I know, of course, my CO came to me and said, Listen, that is a guide-line from Holland. And I would not likely be too -- prepared to repeat exactly what I said in this court because that would be inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I understand you. Can you tell us, now that we -- so that we don't have to go into that any deeper, whether your battalion, when it carried out the order to take those blocking positions, was it in a position to actually defend Srebrenica? Did it have enough strength to defend Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A simple and short answer: No. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So did you knowingly do that task counting that there would be air support?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told before, that I personally did not believe in air support any more, after the air support comedy about OP Echo I told you about, asking for airplanes were not available, et cetera. No, I did not count on air support. I was very happy to hear later on that there would be air support, which, after all, did not come. I refer to the air-strike situation on the morning of the 11th. But I just did it with the means I had and hoped the best for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As you received the order to set up blocking positions regardless of the fact that you couldn't defend the town, given the -- your strength, as you could see, the Republika Srpska army was issued orders by the corps commander General Zivanovic not to open fire on UNPROFOR on the 8th. Now I'm asking you this: You obeyed the orders that you received, they obeyed the orders that they received, but because the VRS did not fire on UNPROFOR on the 9th, the 10th, and the 11th, did it result in the postponement of mass air-strikes? Was that the reason why there were no mass air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with the last question, I really don't know where there were no air-strikes because, again, I thought that our request responded to all the conditions the UN had. Then you say that the VRS obeyed the orders, et cetera. We discussed that last week, that there was firing of VRS on UN positions. And when you told me that they were ordered not to, I told you that then obviously they did not follow their orders. I think that answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I need you to answer the following question for me: Setting up the blocking positions of UNPROFOR to the south of the enclave, was the sole purpose of that to provoke the Republika Srpska army into attacking UNPROFOR troops which was to result in the NATO air-strikes targeting the Republika Srpska army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you a couple of minutes ago, the purpose of those blocking positions was to prevent the VRS to enter the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this have anything to do with the wish to ensure that there would be NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think, repeatedly, the witness has answered this question. It's really a repetition. Carry on with another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, since you've answered this question and the Trial Chamber is cognizant of it, I would now like us to move on to another topic and that's the convoys, smuggling of humanitarian aid, and the conflicts of UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and so on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, in that case, if you are really moving to another topic, it is a convenient time, I think, for a break now, the first break, on technical reasons, to rewound the tapes. We have our first break now and resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, at the beginning of the testimony of this witness, you indicated you need ten hours for cross-examination. At the end of today's hearing, you will have used approximately nine hours. I am told that the witness has a problem to come back to the court tomorrow if we don't finish today. Could you indicate if it is possible to finish with the examination of this witness today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Considering what you've just said, I will try and I will ask the witness to answer as briefly as possible, and then we will most probably manage to complete this today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have an additional idea: To avoid any repetition of a question would save time as well. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, in the summary, both in the Popovic case and here, called the control of the convoys at terror against the convoys. Can you tell us, What were the various difficulties that you had, considering everything that you said in the transcript in the Popovic case 3322 and 3323, in these pages? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. As a battalion, we had our logistic needs, and they were to be addressed to by coming in logistic convoys from our logistic base in the area of Busovaca. The procedure was, when we arrived, that every time we wanted a convoy to come in, there has to be the consent of the VRS, not only about the fact that the convoy came and when it came, but even about the contents of that convoy. And because on one hand the convoys were refused many, many times and then even the contents were refused or partially refused, we could not meet our logistic needs. And that's what I meant by calling it convoy terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you mean just the convoys that had to do with UNPROFOR or do you also imply the UNHCR convoys? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was concerning my convoys, so the UNPROFOR convoys. I know about the fact that UNHCR had problems, but I don't know about details, these convoys, concerning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the restrictions that are implied in your answer, namely obtaining equipment by the convoys, did this imply restrictions that had to do with weapons, ammunition, and other materiel, which is called the technical equipment for equipping vehicles and other combat equipment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to do with that as well; but for food and fuel, et cetera, the same problem was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic case on page 3323, lines 3 to 5 of the transcript, in your testimony you said -- I apologise. In the summary of your testimony on page 3323 in lines 3 to 5 in the transcript in the Popovic case - this is the summary of your testimony read out by the OTP - it is emphasised that you said how the weapons and ammunition of the Dutch Battalion were reduced and became inoperative because the VRS restricted convoy access because there was a need to maintain and replace some of the equipment. So does your assessment follow what you mention in this summary read out in the Popovic case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm not sure if the page is the right one. I don't think so because I have a different page number of the Popovic transcript. And the second is: The summary read out by the OTP is not part of the evidence. To be able to follow what you are putting to the witness, we would like to know the exact reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If you remember, Mr. President, on the first day of the testimony of this witness, the Prosecutor read out the summary of his testimony in the Popovic case. Therefore, on page 3323 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is quite different. You said the Popovic -- you were quoting the Popovic transcript. Now you are quoting the transcript of this trial. Thank you. That clarifies the situation. What is the question for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do apologise. My mistake. I am sorry for causing confusion. Let me repeat what the Prosecutor has said. They said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please don't repeat. Just put a question to the witness. You have read it into the transcript and now put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, What were the weapons that in a short period of just a few months became inoperative and could not be used any longer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First remark: It does not concern a short period of a few months because we took over the equipment of DutchBat II and those limitations to convoys already existed in the period they were there. Then to answer your question, I can give you some examples. Even my rifles were -- to explain that, I'm getting technical, but even my rifles need repair. All my anti-tank systems should have been tested and repaired. Ammunition for my mortars and ammunition for my anti-tank systems was put out of action by the influence of moisture, and so I can give quite a lot. But the fact is concern about all my weapons systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether these systems were used to attack until the moment when the green signal was issued? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, none of my systems were used to attack. And having stated that they were not operational, I not even could use them in defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Then please tell us, What was the average consumption of ammunition of the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica, and where was this ammunition used?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know numbers about the average consumption because in the period that there was actual contact with the VRS, it could have been reported but not on the command net, and I was not interested at that very moment. I ordered that within the unit they had to change numbers of available ammunition or exchange, change between the platoons so that everybody got some ammunition. I can tell you that [indiscernible] and I were a logistic report; we had not more than 16 per cent of the ammunition we should have had in the beginning. And ammunition is not only used by firing it, but keeping it long in the open, not in the proper packages, ammunition devaluates as well, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether your needs to obtain ammunition and reserve parts for weapons are consistent with the period in March and April, or is another month in question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question. But the fact is there -- when we came there and we took over from DutchBat II, we had already a big need for ammo, spare parts, et cetera, and that just increased during the period we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the requests you made until the month of May, let's say, 1995, did you request that the weapons systems, the ammo, and the weapons be replaced, or did this only happen after the month of May? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It started to happen in January and all the first requests, and it stayed the whole period that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic case, as stated in the summary of your testimonies in this case, which the OTP read out, you said that the battalion did not have sufficient ammo and other military equipment; is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And that is in fact what we said, that we took over at a too-low level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is the following: Can you tell us as an officer whether it is reasonable to allow armed forces to arm themselves, even if these are UNPROFOR forces, if there is a danger that the weapons might be used against you, whether by being seised by members of the BiH army, and there were instances of that, of which we warned the UNPROFOR, or if the UNPROFOR would use these weapons against you because, as you told us, the VRS was viewed as the aggressor? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To start with, UNPROFOR was within the enclave with the consent of both parties. Even in the face that that was so, there were limitations to whatever could be brought into the enclave. If you are there as an UNPROFOR force with the consent of both parties, I do not understand that there would have been a fear that we should use those weapons against you, and I think you mean VRS. Because they were aware of our orders, and we just had to deter any party by presence, and we did not -- and within our mandate there was not in any way the possibility that we would attack or whatever or start firing upon any of the parties. Then again, whether I think it's reasonable for any party to think whatever, I don't think that is applicable. If you are there in an enclave with the consent of both parties, I do not understand why you do not allow to get the unit, in fact, working for you as well in a phase, to get the supplies he needs. And not only army and equipment, because, again, even food and even blood was rejected. And blood, not to eat, but for our dressing station, for our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether this was usual after the month of May when the air-strikes were carried out against the centre of Republika Srpska, Pale and so on, that we should allow the UNPROFOR to arm themselves in order -- in accordance with their requests, while, on the other hand, the UNPROFOR and NATO used weapons only against Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the fact -- or stating that the situation in Srebrenica, being in an isolated location, I can't react on the fact that something was usual because it was a very unusual situation. And then again, I've just given evidence of the fact that we were a subject of what I called convoy terror. Justifying the one way or the other way, telling you and the Court that we didn't get the supplies and everything else we needed to do our job, is just what I mean in my answers. And any justification or arguments or conditions or thoughts by any party, sorry, I can't answer that. And I don't think it's applicable for me to answer that. I'm just stating we got too less stuff of anything. That was the reason that, in the end, the situation of the battalion was bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Last Thursday, we saw, and you said in the interview, and General Gvero said while he talked with General Nicolai, and I also told him, that in Zepa a number of APCs were stolen and that the unit in Zepa had five APCs missing. If one combat vehicle such as APC is stolen, and it's not easy to hide one, is it possible that other weapons systems that are smaller might be stolen as well? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is possible, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it then justified for Republika Srpska not to give the weapons to those who might lose them, such as the APCs were lost? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I come back to one answer I gave you before. I'm just giving the -- one of the causes or the reasons why our operational situation was as bad as it was. Cause was that VRS didn't allow anything we wanted to come in. And what the reasons for the VRS were, whether they were justified or not, sorry, I can't be and I don't want to be the judge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see 1D173. While we are waiting for it appear on the screen. Let me say what it is. It's an order from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska dated the 28th of February, 1995, from which one can see that the VRS assessed that the BH Army would begin offensive operations. And the document is signed by General Manojlo Milovanovic. Let's see what it says. We can see that it's a short document, and I only intend to read out something from the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Having monitored the situation and then an assessment of the intentions and capabilities of the Muslim forces, I believe that they will not respect the signed cease-fire and cessation of hostilities for four months but will begin in early March their announced spring offensive and will, as part of it, attempt to link up the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves and then direct their forces towards Kladanj, Olovo, and Tuzla." My question, based on this, is as follows: According to information you had, was this assessment made by General Milovanovic in February justified, and did the so-called spring offensive begin in the month of March? Many witnesses have said here that for 20 days there was an attack carry out from Sarajevo against Ilidza, and there were also sabotage activities of the Muslims who reported that they had killed 60 members of the VRS and so on and so forth. They were doing it from the enclave in which you were. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, we were on a -- pretty isolated, and I did not know or I believe I did not have this information you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any references from your command in Sarajevo about the complaints of the Army of Republika Srpska to the effect that attacks were being carried out from the Srebrenica enclave against the surrounding areas and the population? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember, that in two cases we had contact with the liaison of the VRS, being in this case Major Nikolic of the Bratunac Brigade, which on one occasion complained about an action the Muslims would have taken in the area north of the enclave, that coped with a report of my observation post Mike about battle noise and, by daylight, smoke north of the enclave. We asked then Major Nikolic whether we were allowed to go down there and get the information he has about how many and do you know where they came from, because we didn't see them. Well, you know the problems we had with the location of the OPs. And second occasion, he came with -- an incident that took place south of the enclave, having an ambush by the BiH, by the Muslim army in that area, and in that ambush, as I recollect well, 10 or 12 Serb soldiers were killed. In the last case, we asked him to provide or allow us to get in more material so we could build more OPs in the southern edge. We already had Kilo and Delta new, but we needed more there because we could not control that hilly area without building up more OPs. But then the logistics for building an OP were, again, rejected by the VRS. So that's two occasions that I recollect that were reported to me and that led to complaints by the VRS to the battalion itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us whether you and your monitors noticed that in the spring the Muslims intensified the carrying out of the so-called sabotage activities and the control of the Zepa-Srebrenica corridor? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: About control of the Zepa-Srebrenica corridor, I do not anything about. And as far as the other part of your question is concerned, I think I already answered that in my answer in the last question. I know of -- actually of two events well described to you in the answer I gave you on my last -- on your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you then tell me whether you ever had the occasion during your mandate and your stay in Srebrenica to learn that Muslims were taking away the weapons and the equipment of UNPROFOR? Were there any such incidents, and did you ever report about them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the equipment of UNPROFOR, the equipment of the battalion, then the answer is that the only case where that was done, the only occasion that that was done when they took over or they attacked OP Charlie and that was, as call it in the end phase, there were attempts to steal equipment from observation posts. They were, as far as I know, denied. Two exceptions, but that concerned two small tanks with diesel. If you mean UNPROFOR, the total one, I already told you that I found back a report but not exclusively but within the logistic report system that the Ukrainian unit in Zepa lost five APCs that were reported stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like us to look at your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P607. Page 1 in the English language, that's page 2 in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at the second paragraph, where it says: "During the first few months of our stay, there were very view incidents worth mentioning." That's a brief description of the first period. And then it goes on to say in the third paragraph: "In this period, there was a proposal by the Serbs to do business with the Muslims..." And then you go on to say: "When I say business, I mean business in everything except weapons." Then we go on to the fourth paragraph. You say: "This jibed with our idea of how the relationship between the warring factions should be normalised." Thank you. End of quote. Now, I would like to ask you what you can say about this situation and how long it persisted during your stay in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it you refer to the situation of the trade between both parties? Well, it never came to a practice, as stated there as well. In the end it was denied, and as I remember it, it was denied or it was forbidden by the staff of the 28th Division, so we came very far in details, negotiating that the Serbs would provide the enclave, the Muslim population, with all kinds of stuff, being food, et cetera, et cetera. And then in the end of that procedure, when we came to a de facto decision when it would take place for the first time, the Muslims said, No, we reject it, we won't do it, et cetera. And to my information I got then from the local population, the staff of the 28th Division forbade that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 5 - could you please look at it - you say that this situation continued by the end of May and that by the end of May the parties came into conflict because of all sorts of things. Can you please explain to us what you mean? How come that the two sides parted ways here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to read your question. Moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 5 of your statement and then please give us your answer.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think you are referring to paragraph 2 of this second page or at least the page I see now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, that is the right part, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is correct. By the end of May, there were more conflicts between both parties. And what I meant by this is what I reported before, increasing close firing, firing, et cetera, et cetera. So, light hostilities. That is what I mean came into conflict.
