And it was, of course, then, completely impossible to come to an agreement. And I suppose the agreement refers to that trade agreement we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And, now, these conflicts that you talk about, the skirmishes, are you talking about the two, both sides, until the end of May, or was it something that was characteristic of just one side? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The skirmishes firing, the increasing close firing and firing at the enclave, was done at VRS, but in that period we -- I was reported that there was fire with small arms from outside the enclave -- or from inside the enclave in the direction of the VRS as well. And that is what I meant with increasing the skirmishing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us whether in this time-period the sabotage activities were stepped up? I'm talking about those activities launched from inside of the enclave towards the outside of the enclave. You did not answer my question when I asked you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to answer now. As I told you before, I know of two cases of actual actions of the ABiH where the VRS complained about to the battalion. So whether actions stepped up or increased or whatever, I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 1D182. I'm interested in paragraph 2, line 1 and line 2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D52.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, we can see here, the date is the 8th of July, 1995, and the place is Tuzla. And the 2nd Corps command states as following: "60 Chetniks were killed. And according to unconfirmed reports, the aggressor suffered even greater losses and had many wounded." And then he goes on to say how many weapons of what kind were seised. The third paragraph goes on to say: "In the village of Visnjica, large quantities of ammunition were seised, but the soldiers were exhausted, and it was impossible to remove all of it, so the ammunition was destroyed, as were all the facilities that the aggressor could have used for military purposes." Thank you. End of quote. Now, my question based on this is the following: Were you aware of it, and were you able to hear the explosions? Were you able to hear the exchange of gun-fire? Because these are all areas close to you and the whole village was burnt down. Were you able to see those houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your first question, I was not aware of it, at least not this result. And to answer your next question, I'm sorry, but I do not know where that village is by head, probably knew 15 years ago but not now. And it could comply with the report or the report I got of that smoke and battle noise by OP Mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your view, the number of 60 villagers killed in an action launched from inside of the so-called demilitarised zone, the enclave, is it a great number or a small number? And is it something that is actually permissible or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your last question, in any conflict it is never authorised or permissible to kill civilians, if that number of 60 refers to civilians, of course. And if it's a great number, yes, it's a massive number, but, again, you have to make some - how do you call it? - to see it in a context. Because, one, I don't know the village, I don't know how many people were there were, I don't know how big the attacking force was, and I don't know whether and in what way it was defended. So in that case ... But when it concerns killing civilians, even one is a great number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw when I read this out a little while ago that this was a report on operations launched by sabotage and reconnaissance units that were infiltrated, that infiltrated the territory controlled by the Republika Srpska army from the protected areas. So they were not involved in operations at the front to inflict those casualties, but they inflicted casualties. They killed and wounded whoever they encountered on the axis of their advance of their attack, civilians or otherwise. Did you ever discuss those protests made by Nikolic or by other people sent through the Sarajevo command of UNPROFOR about the military operations launched by the demilitarised zone in Srebrenica with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, first, you suggest that those actions were taken from out the enclave, so from out the UN protected zone. I do not know whether that is correct. But the two complaints we got were by Major Nikolic were passed through to our higher echelon, reported, and those complaints were put down at the staff of 28th Division as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever disarm the BH Army units in Srebrenica? And that was part of your mandate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First don't -- as far as I'm concerned, the demilitarisation of the enclave, I stated that before. We did not manage to do that. And we did by occasion, and, again, I have to dig in my memory, but on two or three occasions we managed to block BiH patrol and took their weapons and brought them to the WPC, weapon collection point, where the other weapons from the Muslims were as well, in custody of the UN. That was within the compound of B Company within the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell us, because I want to go back to our basic topic and that's corruption and weapon smuggling, which groups controlled the black-market that you speak about in your statement? And if you need me, I will quote from it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never found proof who controlled it, but we were convinced of the fact that it couldn't exist without the consent or even co-operation of both military and civil authorities within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell me, What goods were traded on the black-market?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what, but what we could see was that there were cigarettes, sometimes - what do you call that? - well, food issues, et cetera. Things like that were traded at the black-market. But that was the open black-market in the actual market in the city of Srebrenica. What all happened back doors or wherever in other location, I do not know of what the contents of that were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So these were food and items such as clothing. What actually could be bought at this open-air market that you are talking about -- or, rather, black-market?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, as I told you, cigarettes, sometimes certain food articles. I don't remember clothing, but mostly that were the subjects that could be bought in open on the market in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether there were items that had come in on the humanitarian aid convoys that were traded on this open black-market? After all, your unit conducted controls of those convoys. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I can't. We never had proof or -- that it came in with humanitarian aid convoys, for instance, UNHCR, and my control of the convoys was very limited. The only control I had was that we were ordered to accompany them from OP Papa, so the northern entrance of the enclave, to the warehouse where we secured them during the unpacking of the trucks. And then it was up to the opstina, the civil authorities, to divide it or distribute it, et cetera. So I did not -- never have exact -- sorry, I knew on paper what was in the convoys, I had no reason to believe that there was anything else in the convoys, and I never found that there was anything else in the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like us to look at document 1D034, where Muslims themselves speak about the black-market. It's a document entitled, "Analytical Overview on the Causes of the Fall of Srebrenica and Zepa," sent by the brigadier-general of the BH Army, General Jusuf Jasarevic, commander of the Main Staff -- to the commander of the Main Staff of the BH Army, Rasim Delic. Could you please look at page of this document and tell us what is stated there. Okay. Yes. We can see the third paragraph: "The international players' calculation and indecision regarding the safe areas and smuggling and profiteering by members of UNPROFOR were also a factor which had a significant impact on the overall security situation in Srebrenica and Zepa." So could you please tell us whether this analysis presented by the brigadier-general, who was a commander in the BH Army, really was relevant for the situation in Zepa and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as Zepa is concerned, I couldn't say anything, of course, because I do not know anything about the situation, then, in Zepa. And if a BiH general concludes something out of his knowledge, et cetera, well, again, don't ask me for it. The total thing, conclusion, well, it is his conclusion. And what do you want me to say about that? I don't share it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And you tell me, then, whether you have any knowledge of the smuggling and profiteering by the UNPROFOR members as described here by the brigadier-general? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean UNPROFOR members being members of DutchBat, we had one event where we discovered smuggling, and the soldier that took part of that, is, according to our rules, punished and prosecuted. And further, we would -- I do not know about any events that members of DutchBat are engaged with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us what that soldier actually smuggled and when it happened? I'm talking about the year and the month.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The year is obviously 1995. It concerned a pretty vast amount of money. About - what was it? - about 300.000 Deutschemarks, and it was contained in canned soup. And we found that because, due to limitations to leave convoys, quite a lot of our guys were in Zagreb and couldn't return. But miraculously before, during their leave, there came in packages sent by the families. And as the battalion had a pretty severe shortage of food, we decided to use the food in those packages sent by the family. And to our surprise in one of the packages we opened it and thought we would find tomato soup, which was incorrect. We found many Deutschemarks. And that is the only actual case that I -- the Deutschemarks were - there was a list with names - meant for local Muslims. And that's the only event that I -- that we found proof of smuggling by DutchBat members.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 4 of this document that we have here in e-court. And I would like to thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 2, where it says: "Among the residents of Srebrenica, there is an ever-increasing mistrust towards the civilian and military leadership fostered by or fermented by the unjust distribution and various mechanations [as interpreted] with the humanitarian relief. And Naser Oric and the municipal officials Osman Suljic, Adem Salihovic, and Hamdija Fejzic were involved in that. There are reports, intelligence, indicating that these people smuggled humanitarian relief, weapons, oil, and so on, and that in their smuggling activities they worked together with the UNPROFOR and what they called the aggressor." So my question to you is this: Several names are mentioned here, and UNPROFOR is mentioned too. So what can you tell us about this, and are you familiar with these names and these people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard the names. I couldn't find them as -- oh, yeah, I see them now. No, those names are not familiar to me, except, of course, the name of Naser Oric, being the commander of the 28th Division. And then your second question is UNPROFOR is mentioned too. Well, again, as I stated before, I know of one case that we found out that personnel or a soldier of DutchBat was guilty of smuggling, and, well, we took our proper measurements. But further on there were no indications even or rumours that that was done by more members than that one soldier who was punished. As far as the VRS was involved, there's just one occasion that I know of - I don't mean the rumours, because there were a lot of rumours - that is, when we contacted an empty Pony Express - I explained to you last week - with some guards with it, at the moment we contacted them or we stopped them they were unarmed, and we asked them, Where are you coming from? And he pointed down south in the direction of Zepa, because that was in the area of OP Delta, and patrol commander asked him, How is that possible, because the VRS is there? Oh, and he said, probably - forgive my pronunciation - Nema problema, Chetniks, no problem, Deutschemarks. That was an indication that VRS personnel was involved as well. But that was the only indication we got more or less an indication or proof of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please tell me whether UNPROFOR controlled humanitarian convoys and whether it had any influence over the distribution of the humanitarian aid inside the enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I take it that in this case you mean by UNPROFOR DutchBat. I told that you that we did not control them, not the contents of them. We saw the papers and there it was reported what was in it. And the only control we did is that it came from the trucks into the warehouse where it was under the control of UNHCR, and they were concerned, together with the opstina, the civil authorities in the enclave, they were responsible for the distribution, et cetera. But there was no role for DutchBat in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me whether you know if the goods brought in as humanitarian aid ended up in the hands of the BH Army, and was it them that decided how it would be distributed and used subsequently?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were rumours about that. One of my officers asked the UNHCR representative about that. He denied, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like 1D034 to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat the number; it's not recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like 1D034 to be admitted into evidence. It's the Muslim report on the situation in the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, but at this stage I would like to note that many of or some of the documents you have used are not in your list we received before court today.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will check why that was the case, and I think this document should be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, in the Popovic case at transcript page 2447, lines 4 through 5, you stated, and I quote: "The battalion needed 8- to 9.000 litres of fuel a day in order to be able to do its job." And then you go on to say: "When the fuel supplies decreased, 250 litres of fuel were used daily." I don't know if I quoted you correctly. Could you please correct me if that is not the case. But if yes, could you please explain why did you need such vast quantities of fuel, 8 to 9.000 litres a day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can't see, because I don't see a document, whether you quoted me correctly, but I think I can answer the question anyway. The battalion needed 8- to 9.000 litres of fuel because we had to do a lot of patrolling. And, in fact, it was meant to be done by APC or, not in the area of the confrontation line, by wheeled vehicle. Secondary, there was no -- any kind -- there was not any kind of energy in the enclave, so no electricity, no drinking water, et cetera, so we had to use generators, et cetera, et cetera, which consumed fuel, to purify our water, to keep up energy for our communications. Well, I can make a whole list, but you can imagine yourself that if you do not have energy at all, you have to raise it yourself, that consumes quite a lot of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you maintain that you needed 9 tonnes [as interpreted] of fuel a day; yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry. Not 9.000 tonnes, but 8- to 9.000 litre of fuel. This is the correct quotation of the transcript in Popovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I made a mistake. I meant 9.000 litres or 9 tonnes of oil. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness has explained that, according to the transcript in Popovic. What are you asking?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness said that he was not sure whether he said 8 or 9 tonnes, so I'm asking him, for the transcript, whether daily they needed 9 tonnes of fuel. However, I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where did you storage the 9 tonnes of fuel a day? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had a fuel storage in the form of big sacks and a couple of tanks on the main -- on each compound. And we had fuel reserves on every OP because they had to raise all their energy as well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any documents from which one can see how the fuel was distributed on a daily basis and what was the consumption and what were the requests for new supplies? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an NCO who was concerned with that, but I really do not recollect or have any papers with this detailed logistic items.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, Is it possible that, if you receive 9 tonnes of fuel a day, a certain part of that might be taken away or end up, as you said, on the black-market? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, your assumption that receiving 9 tonnes of fuel a day -- again, I just stated that my needs were 8- up till 9.000 litres a day. And it is impossible, absolutely impossible, that when it came to our OP Papa, say, within our area of responsibility, that it would end on the black-market. As I stated before, I know of a couple of cases where what we call jerrycans were stolen from OPs with diesel. And where that ended up -- did end up, I do not know of. But properly coming in with a convoy and the amount of diesel coming in at OP Papa, at our north entrance, it's impossible that even a small part of it landed on the black-market or came into the hands of the ABiH or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When there were no restrictions imposed, did you receive the 9 tonnes which was as much as you needed, or were you never receiving that quantity? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember when there were no restrictions imposed, so when I came there the supplies of DutchBat II were diminished already. And I never received an amount of fuel that much that it could cope with my daily need.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, In what way did members of the BH Army in the enclave manage to obtain fuel, if you know that? Was there any legal channel to bring fuel into the enclave which could have been used to supply their army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How they did supply their need for fuel, I do not know. There is a possibility, but we checked that regularly, we supplied fuel for the bakery in the town so it would be possible to make bread for the civilian population in that bakery. And that, in fact, is the only places I remember it, and I think that I am correct, the only spot where -- which was not under our direct control where fuel was present in order to allow the bakery to bake bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now show a video-clip. This is 1D211. And these are short clips from news shows which show that the UNPROFOR and UNHCR convoys were used to smuggle weapons for the needs of the BH Army. We only have the transcript for the first and last part of this video-clip, and therefore I would ask the interpreters to interpret simultaneously into English what is being said. The total length of the clip is about 10 minutes. I would ask the interpreters to interpret from the video-clip directly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For better understanding for the Chamber, it would be helpful to indicate the source of this clip. Where is it from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have said that these are excerpts from news shows which were broadcast publicly and were also presented as exhibits in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: When we do not have the transcript, we normally do not interpret directly from video-clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, could you tell us which TV channel this was taken from, if you know? And do you have the full text in B/C/S of the -- what we are going to hear, for the sake of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have the complete text, and this is why I asked the interpreters to interpret simultaneously for these ten minutes into English so that you could see what it is about. As for the image, it tells for itself. And this was used as an exhibit in the Popovic et al. case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We heard from the interpreters that they normally don't interpret without having the text. It's a question of accuracy of the text, the translation, and the transcript. I hope they can manage it; but if not, you will see what will happen. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This is too quick.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Ammunition was found because there was a double bottom, and this is the second time that it happens in our zone of responsibility. In humanitarian aid, we found aid which consists in weapons and ammunition. Question: Do you know where this ammunition comes from? Answer: It is all produced in Konjic, and it was brought to the Sarajevo airport and then by land. This time it was brought by the French troops who were escorting. From those in authority in UN, we requested an official information, but we couldn't get it because they said they were not authorised. Unofficially, in conversation, UNHCR representatives said that they had nothing to do with these trucks or containers and that they were only responsible for what was carried in the containers. What was under the containers they were not interested in. The representatives of the French UN apologised, saying that they were just the escort, whereas the UN police said that they would investigate and timely inform us about the result. Whoever it was who loaded this at the airport remains a secret for us. How many such convoys have already passed, we do not know, but it is a fact that, once again, we have unmasked UNPROFOR who brings in and distributes weapons and ammunition for Muslims under the cloak of humanitarian aid."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This is just a partial interpretation, as the text is being read out in the news very quickly. [Voiceover] "In the UN convoy which was checked, it was established that the blue helmets have a surplus of weapons. These were five automatic rifles and 20 Zoljas. You can see how the rifles are being discovered. You can see the blue helmets themselves know where they placed the weapons which they were carrying towards Visoko and Kiseljak. And they are not listed in the specification. No automatic rifles or Zoljas are mentioned here. You can see for yourselves how the rifles look. As this trick was unsuccessful, the UN trucks turned back and returned to their base in Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. How they are going to explain to Serbs that this was humanitarian aid to Muslims will be very difficult, especially if one talks about their bias. It would be certainly different if the world new about the real truth in the ground. There were false accusations used by those who should bring back truth and trust into this region. The London Guardian says today that the commander of the UNPROFOR for the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, Michael Rose, sent four members of the British Intelligence Service, rather than military monitors of United Nations, to Gorazde. Once again, the peacekeeping forces had a surplus of weapons today. "Here is a report of our reporters: Yesterday, at about 1700 hours, a convoy moving from Kiseljak to Sarajevo was stopped. It included three APCs, three trucks, and 15 members of the Swedish and Norwegian Battalions. After a regular and routine control, Serbian border policemen found a large amount of explosives, ammunition, and weapons in the vehicles of Swedish soldiers. Today we had a case that there was somewhat more ammunition, anti-tank mines, and 7.62 millimetres, as well as plastic explosive in these vehicles, around 120 kilos. As they have three APCs, that means that the weapons should be different. I doubt that they need explosives and so on. However, they declared they had it, so we can say it's correct. However, these rocket guns, signal ammunition, and so on and so forth, whatever has not been reported, we'll have to seise that, and we'll give them some papers for that. Once they receive an approval from the Main Staff of the VRS, we'll allow them to have it. How did this confusion take place? How can the ... "The convoy is still at the Kobiljaca border post and is waiting for papers and the result of the agreement between the Serbian authorities and the command of UNPROFOR. After that, it will return on its way to Sarajevo or go back to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I just received information that there is no sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We didn't receive any sound for the last couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: I thought that it is a problem in my earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, no. At the beginning, we had no translation. Then the interpreters - and I think we all should be grateful for that - tried to catch as much as possible. And at the end we didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I really do not know what the problem is because this worked until recently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thanks to Aleksandar. I think this is sufficient for me to be able to ask the witness a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please say whether you were aware that in some humanitarian aid convoys weapons were being smuggled, as we could see from these video-clips, even in flour which was intended for the civilian population in the enclaves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. And as far as the area of Srebrenica and the DutchBat is concerning, I am -- I never had report, indications, rumours, or whatever that that took place in my area of responsibility as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To clarify the transcript, on page 61, line 10, Mr. Gajic was speaking. And if I'm -- I was told that the 65 ter number, 1D211, is in fact a book and not a video. You should try to figure out the correct number. And then carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. The correct number is 1D212. And the interpretation of the first and last parts of what is being said in the video-clips are documents 1D216 and 1D217.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would have been helpful to get this information earlier. You wanted to put questions to the witness, Mr. Tolimir; do it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, did you have any instructions that you received from the sector command, the Sector Sarajevo or the Sector Tuzla, that to the effect that the humanitarian convoys are being used to smuggle weapons and military equipment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it usual that the VRS, if it discovered that the convoys were being used as we have just seen now, to put in double bottoms under flour and so on, that it should control and check the convoys which enter enclaves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it that with "usual" you mean logical or comprehensible. Yes, of course, I can imagine, if you have incidents like that, that you want to check whether the contents of a convoy are -- conformed the list of containments presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, as the deputy commander, ever receive information from anyone that a convoy with humanitarian aid is being used to transport weapons and materiel? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated before, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender the video-clip 1D212 and the transcripts of the initial and final parts of this video-clip, namely 1D216 and 1D217 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just want to know when or if we can expect to be provided with any specific information along the lines that Your Honour had asked about pertaining to what these videos actually depict, i.e., dates, locations, what television stations these were being reported over, any particulars so that the Court may be assisted to know whether these particular incidents have any relevance, temporally, geographically, or in any other way to what was going on in Srebrenica and Zepa. As it stands, we have none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your comment on this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In the transcript, which we did not hear, it is stated in which locations this was found and when. And as for the video-clip, I said that these were excerpts from the public media, the public service of the radio and television of Republika Srpska. If we need to describe what is not -- what was not heard here because we had no sound, we will then submit a separate document to the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would just like to add one thing before you rule: This document -- or, rather, this videotape was disclosed to the Defence by the Prosecution, and it was used and admitted into evidence in the Popovic case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the Chamber, there's not enough information about the source and the background and the date this video-clip was taken, so that we will mark it for identification. The Defence may add some information to it and submit it to the Trial Chamber. At this stage of the proceedings, the Chamber is not in the position to receive it as an exhibit on which anybody can rely on. We must have our final break now for today. I would like to know, do you need the whole last 45 minutes for the completion of your examination, or is it possible to leave some time for the Prosecution for re-examination, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will do my best to reduce the number of questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We adjourn and resume a little bit earlier, ten minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Tolimir, the Registrar has to give us a number and I think for all three documents, video and the two transcripts we have seen before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 1D212 is now Exhibit D72, marked for identification. The transcript will be attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now I would like us to look at document 1D213 in the e-court. It's a report drafted by Captain Slavko Novakovic, and the report describes the way in which convoys were controlled, the check-points, the routes, and the way in which those humanitarian aid convoys were put to malicious use.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, well we can see the front page now. It just specifies the locations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we please look at page 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your microphone should be switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like us to look at page 1 of this text -- or, rather, page 2. Because I believe we are now at page 3. So could we please look at page 2. Both in the Serbian language -- or, rather, page 2 in the Serbian language, and page 1, the last paragraph on that page, in the English language.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the last paragraph on page 1 in the Serbian language, it's the next page in the English language. Thank you. I will try -- well, thank you, yes. It says in the last paragraph in the Serbian language and in the English: "Understandably, most cases of attempting smuggling of goods were in the convoys for Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, which had the fewest possibilities for being provisioned, apart from humanitarian aid. The following goods were smuggled in in most of the cases: Video cameras, cameras, films, weapons, radio sets, satellite equipment, and aerial signalling communication equipment, optical devices, night vision devices, engine oil, various parts for devices, anti-freeze, chemical manure, oxygen cylinders, flak jackets, helmets, sleeping bags, military clothing and footwear, and various food stuffs." Please, since you had an opinion on those convoys, I would like, now, to show you the following analysis contained in page 3 of this document. This is an analysis by Captain Slavko Nikovic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please look at page 3. That's the next page. Also in the English language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So it's the third paragraph in the Serb language and also in the English language. When it says: "When the representatives of UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations complain about the procedure of the organs at the check-points, in the majority of the cases, their aim is to use counter-accusations to lessen their own responsibility, owing to the attempts to abuse their humanitarian function and to play fast and loose with the mandate entrusted to them. However, not all of their accusations can be dismissed because our side has not been blameless in the procedure of inspection, which is something that is rarely repeated." So my question based on this is the following: So based on the practice that was prevalent in Srebrenica, can you please comment on this analysis by the captain, and were those items really controlled, and were they, in most cases, the object of controversy in those convoys? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I see it, the analysis of the captain mentioned by you is concerning humanitarian aid. In the case of Srebrenica in the period I was there, these convoys were executed by UNHCR. Stated before, I know not of actual smuggling into the Srebrenica area by UNHCR. I told you before. So ... well, in fact, that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell me whether you, your unit, the DutchBat, whether you controlled the UNHCR convoys in any conditions, or did you at least check the documents that accompanied the convoys? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that happened, and I -- as I said before, I did not actually control the contents of the UNHCR convoys. I told you what the job was we had to do, accompany, secure, til in the warehouse, then UNHCR was responsible for distribution. And we were presented the contents or the -- the papers belonging to that convoy and that the only thing we thought that there was wheat in it or clothing or whatever, any humanitarian thing, and that's all I can answer you to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. He speaks about the things that are contained in humanitarian aid convoys, and he even showed some self-criticism here, saying that there were some omissions, some errors made by the Republika Srpska army when it controlled the convoys. He's not making any accusations against UNPROFOR or UNHCR, he's just talking about the goods, the items in those convoys which were smuggled in most of the cases, and these are goods that were banned. Did you notice, when you carried out your checks, any of those items? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, again, Mr. Tolimir, concerning the UNHCR convoys, I did not check. The only thing I was informed about: What were, according to the papers, the contents of that convoy. But we did not enter the trucks or inspect the undersides of the trucks or whatever. The only thing we did, as I said before, accompany them to the warehouse, secure the unloading, and then UNHCR was responsible for the further actions taken with those supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you notified by the UNHCR that parts of consignments were kept or seised at the check-points manned by the Republika Srpska army on some occasions, and were you told why?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not informed by UNHCR about things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you do not have any complaints about the way in which the UNHCR brought the humanitarian aid into the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When they arrived, they brought stuff that was necessary, as far as I knew and was concerned, necessary for the population, and so I was happy when they came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like this report, this analysis on the UNHCR convoys that reached the enclave, be admitted into evidence since it contains an overview which I did not read out here. And the witness said that he -- or, rather, his officers and soldiers had seen the documents that accompanied the convoys. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to see the first page again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Could we please look at it on the first -- could we please look at page 1 in the e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With some additional information, I don't see a heading of this page. Who is the institution who produced this report? I don't see any date. Can you give some additional information, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I said that this was a report drafted by Captain Slavko Nikolic -- Slavko Novakovic, I'm sorry - showing the way in which convoys were checked. The routes and check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was not my question, Mr. Tolimir. We have that on the record. I asked for something else. Who provided this document? Who produced it? There's no headline. I don't know -- no heading, no date. I have no idea what it is about. And who is Captain Slavko Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain Slavko Novakovic actually carried out the checks of the convoys that reached -- that entered Srebrenica, and he made this analysis at the behest of the Republika Srpska army. And we will see later on some analysis made by General Milovanovic and others for the purpose of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I have to stop you, to save time. This was not the question. Can we please see the last page. Again, I can't see any date of this report. On the left side, in B/C/S, there is a signature. Mr. Franken, do you know a person with a name Slavko Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, do you want to comment on the application of Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the only additional assistance I can lend is I believe this document may be a Drina Corps collection document, but we're in the same boat. We have no idea when this was created. It appears to have been created sometime after 1994; there's reference to 1994. I think Captain Novakovic may have been an officer in the Drina Corps. If my recollection serves, he was a listed Defence witness for one of the Popovic Defendants, but I don't believe he ever testified, so I don't think we actually have any evidence on the record that will assist us further with the providence of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that this document can't be received as an exhibit to date. It will be marked for identification. We have no date. We don't know anything about the institution on behalf of that, this certain Mr. Captain Slavko Novakovic had drafted this document, there's no stamp and no indication about reliability and the source. You may decide, Mr. Tolimir, if you would like to give more information for the Chamber or call Mr. Novakovic as a witness for the Defence at a later stage. Please carry on now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D213 will be Exhibit D73, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now I would like us to look at 1D214. It's a document from the Main Staff of the VRS drafted by Colonel-General Manojlo Milovanovic, the chief of the Main Staff. It's a weekly plan for the deliveries of humanitarian aid between the 13th and 19th of May, 1995. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, we can see here that the convoys left for Srebrenica on the 16th of May. It's the third line here. And again at line 6 it says Karakaj Srebrenica. And then on the 17th of May and so on. The 18th of May. So now I would like to as you this: You have this document in English, and it's actually more legible. We can see from this document that the VRS Main Staff approved the movement of those convoys that carried large quantities of foodstuffs. For instance, on the 15th of May, there were 72 tonnes of flour carried --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what is your question, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply wanted the witness to see the quantities of flour that were being delivered over just two days. And I wanted to ask him if this was restrictive or not, because the witness was speaking of restrictions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The question is: Since we can see from this overview, which I cannot read now, that 72 or 16 tonnes of flour were transported daily, 32 tonnes of flour, 16 tonnes of sugar, and so on, my question is: If Srebrenica had 35.000 of people who depended on humanitarian aid, and we can see that a total of 111 tonnes of flour were approved to be delivered, that means that each person received 3.15 kilos of flour a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are not giving evidence. You are the accused. I'm very sorry to remind you. Put a question to the witness. I haven't heard any question yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Was this how flour was distributed? If -- or, rather, whether this kind of quantity of 3.15 kilos per person was this something that was acceptable as normal, or was it restrictive? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your last question, I don't have the faintest idea. I'm not a professional on this. At least I can conclude that there came in -- probably came in flour in that period for the -- for the population. And your question whether the flour was distributed, I suppose it is. But, then again, UNHCR coped with that and arranged that and there was no role for DutchBat in that distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So my question is whether UNPROFOR in Srebrenica at any point in time sent any requests for greater quantities of humanitarian aid, food for Srebrenica, for its population in relation to the quantities that were actually delivered?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I do not know whether how many times and in what amounts UNPROFOR in Srebrenica - you say -- you mean probably UNHCR in Srebrenica - asked for food for the population. Again, UNPROFOR is not the party who was initiating these kind of convoys. So I can't further answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm happy with your answer. So UNPROFOR did not do that. In this document it shows that a large quantity of materials came in for a major Swedish construction project. Can you tell us something about this major construction project in this area that you -- that was under your control? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it that the one who made this report or this text refers to what I called before the Swedish Shelter Project, being the refugee camp in the south of the enclave I told you about last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please just answer this one more question. As for fuel which arrived for the population in the enclave by humanitarian convoys, what can you tell us about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, lost my ... I know that fuel came in, but still we were providing fuel from our storage for that bakery, so I can't comment on amounts, necessity, daily use of the population, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought not to show a document, but I will. It is 1D215. Can we please see it on the screen. Thank you. Can we please show page 7 of this document in both B/C/S and in English. It is one page from the section entitled "Experience."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see it on the screen now. Just below the word "experience," I will read and quote. It is an interview which you gave on the 13th of September, 1995. This is what it says: "As for the UNHCR, Franken said that, in his view, this organisation, whose aim was to fulfill all its procedures, and thereby losing sight of the actual objective, he failed to understand that they stopped humanitarian aid supplies because they disapproved of the 1.000 litres ever fuel given to the Serbs or because they were searched. An example of this situation was when the BH Army said that they intended to set up roadblocks in the enclave because many white vehicles had been seised by the BSA. Franken said that he would not accept this under any circumstances, and, if necessary, he would prevent it by force. However, in order to avoid an escalation, he offered to subject incoming convoys to a brief inspection by his own staff. This brought about another series of protests from the UNHCR, and two convoys were held back which resulted in aid supplies, including baby food, running out in the enclave. This was used as a coercive measure." My question, based on everything that I just read out, is the following: Can you please clarify for us, now, why the UNHCR protested if the convoys were searched by the UNPROFOR, and what was the specific reason which the UNHCR mentioned in their protest notes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to dig deep in my memory now. The first thing that I did not understand was that they -- at a check-point they were asked to give 1.000 but an amount of fuel to the Serbs and then they went back. And there were other occasions where they reported to me that they had convoys turning back to their original base because they had a reason. Secondly, I indeed remember that I said to the ABiH who claimed that Serb soldiers were coming into the enclave in the vehicles, in white vehicles, which I proclaimed as being nonsense, but then I said, Okay, we'll have a check. Practically the check never took place, but that was a reason for the UNHCR to say we do not want to be checked by you. So if you do that, we will not come anymore. Now, I don't know exactly the period afterwards where I said, Okay, then we won't check; no problem. But I was informed that, on basis of that protest, they stopped about two convoys on their way down to the enclave. I take it this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this protest of UNHCR a reason why the enclave was running out of some crucial foodstuffs, such as the baby food, for example?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The protest was not, as far as I can concede, because that protest was towards DutchBat who had the plan of just make a check, and as -- saying that, that had no influence on the requests on UNHCR convoys nor their contents. Presumably, and that's what I stated before in the document you presented, two convoys were redirected, with which I mean sent back, by the UNHCR. On the very moment or very shortly after, I told them that we would do a quick inspection of the convoys to neutralise the agony at the ABiH site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just briefly tell us, on page 7 of this document, you said, stating your experience about doctors without borders, Medecins Sans Frontieres, you said that some had a positive opinion of it. And then you talk about a Flemish predecessor who was only interested in power politics. What do you think about power politics? In what way was he interested in that? What do you mean to say by this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did mean, that, is - and I'll try to give a short answer - normally an arrange was that civil workers for MSF, Medecins Sans Frontieres, and the DutchBat, a new group would come in, as far as I recollect, the 1st of April. Okay. Why? The opstina wanted everybody as much -- as much -- as much people as possible to be -- to profit from the fact that they had work, either UN base, so they got money and things, et cetera. In April, the Medecins Sans Frontieres refused that. They did not want that. Then there was a conflict between the opstina and Medecins Sans Frontieres, and that escalated more or less, resulting in the fact that -- that the MSF was stopping any medical aid to the civil hospital or to the population because they wanted it the way they thought it should be. Nevertheless, the fact that there was an arrangement and it was arranged that 1st of April, we would change personnel. That's what I meant when, an issue like this, you let it prevail over the humanitarian aid. Then you are doing politics and you are not delivering humanitarian aid. A successor was quite different type who had the humanitarian aid high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a question for the witness. At page 75, line 20 to 23. "... I don't know exactly the period afterwards where I said, Okay ..." I just want to ask about the protests by UNHCR that you mentioned in that paragraph. For how long was the protest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, as I recollect, Your Honour, it was one protest at our HQ. And the consequences lasted about two or three days because then the question was cleared. In that period of two or three days, I later on heard that two convoys were sent back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Then a follow-up question: Two convoys were redirected, which means that they were sent away from the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So the supplies were never -- never reached the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that. But the supplies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- on that moment did not arrive, as planned, in the enclave. That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So we would finish, as requested, because you have some obligations. I just have one additional question. Did you personally or your soldiers or your predecessors who were there before you have any knowledge about military equipment and weapons being thrown by parachute into Srebrenica or that Srebrenica was being armed via the Tuzla airport? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak for myself and eventually reports I got about that. Thrown by parachute, no. I know it is possible, even radiographic controlled parachutes exist. Never had a report that or had, myself, knowledge of that. Being armed through Tuzla airport, I told you about -- or last week already we spoke about that unknown or unidentified Hercules planes coming down in Tuzla, and a good week or ten days later we saw new weapons in Tuzla. And there was a link laid by me then in my interview I gave, but, then again, I said it is an assumption. It was -- I don't have any proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any knowledge as to whether the new weapons which appeared in Tuzla were being supplied to the enclaves, either Zepa or Srebrenica, in any way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I did not know the contents of that mysterious Hercules planes. Then, secondly, I can't tell whether, if there were weapons in there, those weapons went to our enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your detailed answers. Excuse me for asking you many things that I'm interested in, because they are the reasons for which I'm here. Thank you. I wish you all the best in your future life and work. God bless you. That was all from me. Thank you, Mr. President. Thanks to the interpreters who attempted to interpret even what was very fast in the video-clip. Thanks, everyone who helped the Defence today on behalf of the Defence. Thank you for the assistance you provided. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. When you were saying, "Excuse me for asking you many things that I'm interested in ..." I can only agree with you. This is your right. This is the purpose of every examination, especially your cross-examination. Mr. Thayer, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll try to compress it to the seven minutes I have. Good evening, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to pick up on a question that Her Honour Judge Nyambe asked you a moment ago. And if -- well, I think we may have lost the document that was up on the screen that led to that question, but you just referred to two convoys which were redirected away from the enclave, and I'll just quote from the document that was up there. There it is again. "It resulted in aid supplies, including baby food, running out in the enclave." Okay. Now, what does -- based on your experience, can you give the Trial Chamber some idea, using this as a potential example, of how scarce the humanitarian aid was in Srebrenica during this period? And we'll just talk about the period when you were there up through July of 1995. And I don't need you to give us a month-by-month, but let's just focus for the time being before the VRS attack in July of 1995. Can you give the Trial Chamber a sense of what the humanitarian situation was like.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I would speak generally of about those six or seven months we were there, it was at the minimum level or less. Once in a while a peak, but then much too short. If we are speaking about the period, say July, it was devastating. As far as I know, and I'm supposed to know that, there was no food supplies any more available. There was hardly any medical supplies available. There was no water available. Consequence of the lack of medical supplies was that a major part of the population, when they arrived in what I call the little safe area in Potocari, was exhausted, sick, or in any other way damaged. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Colonel. So, based on your experience, if even a single convoy were denied by the VRS, could that have and did that have an effect on the humanitarian situation in Srebrenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the levels were very low. And every time something did not come in, it meant that the situation became worse, directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during your time in Srebrenica, you've testified about contacts with Momir Nikolic, for example, did you receive any complaints, whether it be from Momir Nikolic or any other VRS representative, that UNHCR convoys or UNPROFOR convoys were being abused in any way in terms of smuggling goods?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on your experience with Momir Nikolic and other VRS representatives, had there been such an incident, would they have reported that kind of thing to you, based on your experience, and complained?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would have been very happy to do that, loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General Tolimir asked you some questions about trying to foster trade between the Serb and the Muslim communities in the enclave. Let me just ask you, Colonel: What would have been the simplest way to ensure that the civilian population in Srebrenica had more than the minimum or below the minimum amount of basic foodstuffs and amenities to make their life less miserable?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No limitations to any humanitarian aid convoys. That's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you back to the VRS attack on the enclave. For the record, you testified in the Popovic case at transcript page 2457 about the first couple of days of the attack. The focus on OP Foxtrot we've heard a lot about, and you also testified, and this is at line 13, that Bravo Company reported random shelling of the city. And you later testified on that same page that you received reports of civilian casualties and that UNPROFOR assisted in transporting those wounded. What I want to ask you about is: There was a lot of testimony, a lot of questions, about what happened from the period of 9 July forward, after you issued the green order. You testified today about a point at which Serb infantry could be seen approaching the town of Srebrenica. The first question I have is: Prior to you issuing the green order, did you receive reports of shelling of the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not only of the town, but of another village, as I remember as well. The village of Slatina was pretty massively sheltered -- shelled, I mean, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from the reports that you were receiving, was there any military justification for that shelling?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For Slatina, I can't comment because in the direct neighbourhood of Slatina there were BiH units. So I don't know whether, during the shelling, they were present. For Srebrenica, I can't comment because, of course, there were -- there was one legitimate military target in Srebrenica, the post office being HQ of 28th Division, but the way the city was shelled, that was absolutely the complete surroundings of the city or the city itself, the complete city. Then you must shoot at random, because if you aim at the post office, you can't have massive detonations about 7-, 800 metres away from your target. That is absolutely military scene nonsense. And that happened before the green order as well. And I don't know whether the green order is taken as a change in events because parties didn't know I issued a green order.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So from where you stood, receiving these reports, prior to you issuing that green order, was the town of Srebrenica attacked by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact it was. By artillery mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a lot of questions about whether the blocking position order had been given in order to provoke the VRS into attacking UNPROFOR. I want to first ask you a little bit -- ask to you provide a little bit of context to those questions. And in order to do that, let me just quote to you from your parliamentary testimony where you were talking about this very topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is at page 0308-0482 of the English, which is page 28 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But let me just quote to you a question and answer. You were asked the question: "Was the purpose of taking up blocking positions to draw fire in order that way to get air support, or would they also have been sufficient if the Bosnian Serbs crossed the imaginary line, horizontal 84 it was called?" Your answer was: "What was becoming more important was the smoking gun principle. It went roughly like this: We will only deploy air support if it is clear who has been shot at and with what weapons system. The purpose of the battalion's blocking positions what certainly to ensure that we would stay between the Serbs and the Muslim population. I have already outlined to you what I actually thought of the defensive assignment in the usual military sense of the word 'defence.' Drawing fire did not require an extra assignment. In effect, we had already been doing it quite happily for weeks. That it was a condition of air support that there should be a smoking gun was no problem at all, since people were shooting at us all the time." So, first, can you just clarify or explain what you meant in your parliamentary testimony in 2002 in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, in fact, it was, given the answer to the same answer I had here, that the purpose was another one as the real purpose the blocking positions had. I say it here in different words, but it comes to the fact that the blocking positions were to prevent the Serbs to enter the city. The whole nonsense of drawing fire, et cetera, et cetera, well, as I say there, we have been, and the population as well, we were under fire during some days. And not only that; we have been under fire, all those close firing reports, increasing during May and June. So that is not applicable. The condition, and that is what I meant before, that there were two conditions I couldn't reproduce in my testimony before. But one of that was a smoking gun, and it is described already there. You can only get air support if somebody is firing at you and you identify it, what it was, and where it was; that's a smoking gun principle. But that was no problem over there. We were under fire by several means, by several guns, and we did report, and we knew their location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be clear for the record about two things: One, whose guns were those?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, VRS guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And two: Was 9 July the first time that UNPROFOR had been targeted by those guns, or had you been targeted prior to 9 July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have been targeted before. The first time that it was not at random but really to a purpose was, in fact, the attack on OP Echo and then go on the attack on Foxtrot, the shelling of the town, the shelling of Bravo 1 up til 4, the blocking positions, et cetera. And the blocking positions were fired at before that green order moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a lot of questions about the Bandiera triangle, all kinds of hypotheticals about what might be hidden there, but let me just get us back to the reality of the situation as it was being reported to you. Did you ever receive any reports of the ABiH using tanks?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How about heavy mortars?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Light mortars we estimated them as 81 millimetres. And then for their mortar, 82 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How about artillery?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How about multiple-launch rocket systems like were aimed at you and being fired at you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During this attack, did you receive any reports whatsoever of ABiH soldiers wearing UNPROFOR equipment or uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General Tolimir asked you some questions about what was a legitimate target at a particular time, specifically whether the UN became a legitimate target of the VRS at a particular time. Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Was it -- is it -- was it legitimate for an armed force to enter a UN-declared safe area by force of arms in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let's be clear about that. No, absolutely not. I was referring to the fact that the VRS shot at our positions in a later phase.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General Tolimir asked you some questions about the legitimacy of taking the DutchBat soldiers as POWs, and you agreed that it might be legitimate to take captive people that you considered your enemy. Let me ask you this: Is it legitimate to threaten those POWs with execution if close air support continued? Is that legitimate, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm cognizant of the time, and I think I'll just leave it where it is and let Colonel Franken go home and maybe catch part of the match tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: His country is deeply involved tonight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in my case, Your Honour, but there are other reasons why I'm not available tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I take it this concludes the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It does, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to thank you, sir, for attending the court again and to help us to assist us to find the truth. You are free to return to your normal activities, and there's no need to come back. Not at this stage. The second is, I would like to thank the interpreters and the court recorder and to all the staff who assisted us for the length of today's hearing. I apologise for that. And I apologise to the parties. I think you both are not very happy about some time restraints. But, on the other hand, Mr. Tolimir indicated ten hours, he used approximately eight hours, thank you for that. It was -- and the Prosecution was also under some pressure. In future, we should -- perhaps, the parties should liaise a little bit more effectively about the use of time. If a witness is only available a certain day, then the Chamber itself feels under a certain pressure to come to an end with the examination perhaps a little bit earlier than indicated. I hope with these words we can leave it for today. And we resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. I think in Courtroom II, but I'm not sure about that. Thank you very much. We adjourn.
